## CodeBase for HTML and JSON 

I chose mystery novels of my choice to be the three books I'll use (disclaimer: I have not read the books :)):\
My chosen attributes are Title, Author, Publication year, Publisher, and ISBN #:\
\
1) Title: **The Silent Patient**\
Author: Alex Michaelides\
Publication year: 2019\
Publisher: Celadon Books\
ISBN: 978-1250301710\
\
2) Title: **The Cuckoo's Calling**\
Author: Robert Galbraith (J.K. Rowling's Pseudonym)\
Publication Year: 2013\
PUblisher: Mulholland Books\
ISBN: 978-0316206860\
\
3) Title: **The President is Missing\
Authors:** James Patterson\
Bill Clinton\
Publication year: 2018\
Publisher: Little, Brown and Company\
ISBN: 978-0316412711\

I've created HTML and JSON files. Will be playing around with R in CodeBase part of the homework.

```{r}
library(rvest)
library(DT)
library(jsonlite)
url<-"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mejaz56/Data-607/HTML-and-JSON-Approach/Books.html"

#function to cleanup the dataframes from mismatch cases, extra space, and commas
my_function <- function(fname) {
   cleandata <- trimws(fname)
   cleandata <- tolower(cleandata)
   cleandata <- gsub("[[:space:]]+", " ", cleandata)
   return(cleandata)
}

#reading in html content
html_content<-read_html(url)

#extracting tables from html content
tables<-html_content%>%html_table()

#reading in JSON
books <- fromJSON("Books.json")

#converting the JSON data into dataframe
JSON_df <- as.data.frame(books$Books)

#converting html table content into a dataframe and saving the result
html_df<- as.data.frame(tables[[1]])

#saving a copy of both dataframes so I can manipulate the data 
JSON_df_copy<-JSON_df
html_df_copy<-html_df


#cleaning up by calling the function to remove extra whitespaces and commas
JSON_df_copy$Title<-my_function(JSON_df$Title)
JSON_df_copy$Authors<- my_function(JSON_df$Authors)
JSON_df_copy$Publisher<-my_function(JSON_df$Publisher)
JSON_df_copy$`Publication Year`<-my_function(JSON_df$`Publication Year`)
JSON_df_copy$ISBN <-my_function(JSON_df$ISBN)

html_df_copy$Title<-my_function(html_df_copy$Title)
html_df_copy$Author<- my_function(html_df_copy$Author)
html_df_copy$Publisher<-my_function(html_df_copy$Publisher)
html_df_copy$ISBN <-my_function(html_df_copy$ISBN)

JSON_df_copy$Authors <- my_function(
  gsub("[,;]", " ", JSON_df$Authors)
)

html_df_copy$Author <- my_function(
  gsub("[,;]", " ", html_df$Author)
)


title<-JSON_df_copy$Title==html_df_copy$Title
Author<-JSON_df_copy$Authors == html_df_copy$Author
PY<-JSON_df$`Publication Year`==html_df$`Publication Year`
Publisher<-JSON_df_copy$Publisher ==  html_df_copy$Publisher

ISBN <- gsub("[-[:space:]]", "", JSON_df_copy$ISBN) ==
        gsub("[-[:space:]]", "", html_df_copy$ISBN)


```

## *Presenting the result of comparison*

(with the help of ChatGPT)

```{r}

comparison <- data.frame(
  Attribute = c("Title", "Author", "Publication Year", "Publisher", "ISBN"),
  Result = c(
    paste(title, collapse = "  "),
    paste(Author, collapse = "  "),
    paste(PY, collapse = "  "),
    paste(Publisher, collapse = "  "),
    paste(ISBN, collapse = "  ")
  ),
  Meaning = c(
    "All three titles match",
    "All three authors match",
    "All three years match",
    "All three publishers match",
    "All match"
  )
)

knitr::kable(comparison, caption = "HTML and JSON Comparison")

all.equal(JSON_df_copy, html_df_copy)


```

# Conclusion

Instead of using all.equal, I used == and function to compare individual observation and the tables' contents. It gave me more control. I later did compare the data/tables by all.equal, the result did show that even if the content was identical, the all.equal gave me different result due to data types and column names.
